opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting trend, and I don't think it's so much a reversal as a rebalancing. For the last ten or fifteen years the default answer for almost any workload was "move it to the cloud," and that made a lot of sense when you were talking about general-purpose compute, web services, databases. But AI changes the calculus in a few important ways.

The first is data. When enterprises start doing serious AI work, especially inference on their own proprietary data, that data becomes the crown jewel. Financial institutions, healthcare companies, manufacturers: they're increasingly uncomfortable shipping their most sensitive information out to a third party and having it processed somewhere they don't fully control. There are regulatory concerns, sovereignty concerns, and just plain competitive concerns. If your data is your moat, you want to keep it close.

The second is cost, and this is where it gets really interesting from where I sit. Training is episodic: you do a big run, and then you're done for a while. Renting cloud capacity for that is pretty reasonable. Inference is different. Inference is the ongoing, always-on cost of actually using AI in your business. Once you deploy a model into production and it's serving customers or employees every day, that bill just keeps running. A lot of enterprises are doing the math and realizing that at steady-state volume, owning the infrastructure is far more economical than renting it indefinitely.

The third piece is latency and control. As AI moves into more interactive applications like agents, copilots, and real-time decision-making, response time really matters. Having compute close to where the data and users are gives you a lot more control over that experience, and over the whole stack.

Now, I want to be clear: the cloud isn't going away. The hyperscalers are going to remain enormous, and for experimentation and burst capacity they're fantastic. What we're going to see is a hybrid world, where enterprises experiment in the cloud and then, as workloads mature and become predictable, bring a meaningful chunk of that inference on-prem or into colocation facilities they control.

And the thing that makes that possible, frankly, is efficiency. If running inference requires racks of extremely power-hungry hardware and exotic cooling, most enterprise data centers simply can't accommodate it. They weren't built for that. So the real enabler of this shift is inference-optimized hardware that delivers great performance per watt and per dollar, something that can actually slot into the power and space envelopes enterprises already have. That's a big part of why we think this is the moment for purpose-built inference solutions. The demand is clearly there; the question is whether the infrastructure can meet enterprises where they are.

r001.rationale: The response frames the trend as a rebalancing and says mature inference workloads are brought on-prem, rather than attributing on-premises computing to workloads that never moved to the cloud.

r002.rationale: It says enterprises are uncomfortable sending sensitive proprietary data to third parties and want to keep it close, citing regulatory, sovereignty, and competitive concerns.

r003.rationale: The response says AI changes the infrastructure calculus and leads enterprises to move mature inference workloads on-prem; it does not describe AI as an overlay that leaves application locations unchanged.

r004.rationale: It does not compare the pace of AI integration in cloud offerings with integration into enterprises’ internal applications.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one of the more interesting things happening right now. For about fifteen years the story was everything goes to the cloud, and that made a lot of sense when the dominant workload was web apps and storage and bursty compute. AI changes the economics in a few ways.

The first is just cost. If you're a large enterprise and you're running inference at scale, not training a frontier model, but actually serving models to your employees or your customers all day, every day, that's a very steady, predictable load. And steady, predictable load is exactly the case where owning the hardware beats renting it. The cloud premium is worth paying for elasticity. It's not worth paying when you know you'll be at eighty percent utilization for the next three years.

The second is data. The real value of AI for an enterprise isn't the model, it's the model applied to their data. And a lot of that data was never in the public cloud to begin with. It sits in on-prem systems, in regulated environments, in places where legal and compliance have strong opinions. Moving the compute to the data is a lot easier than moving the data to the compute, especially when you start layering on sovereignty requirements in Europe and elsewhere.

And the third is supply. For the last couple of years, if you wanted GPUs, you took whatever the hyperscalers would give you, at whatever price, on whatever timeline. That taught a lot of CIOs that depending on one or two vendors for the most strategic capability in the company is a risk. So they're diversifying. Some of that is multi-cloud, and some of it is bringing capacity back in-house where they control the roadmap.

Now, I'd push back a little on the framing that it's a wholesale shift back. I don't think the cloud goes away. What I think we end up with is a much more deliberate split. You'll train in the cloud, you'll experiment in the cloud, you'll burst to the cloud. But the workloads that are mature, high volume, and sitting next to sensitive data, those increasingly run in private or co-located data centers, and often at the edge, close to where the data is actually generated. It's less a pendulum swinging back and more the industry finally getting precise about which workload belongs where.

From where I sit, the biggest implication is on the hardware side. If inference is moving into enterprise data centers and edge sites, the constraints change. Power, cooling, footprint, and cost per inference matter a lot more than peak FLOPS. That opens the door for architectures that aren't just scaled-down training chips. So I actually see this shift as a healthy thing. It pushes the market toward purpose-built, efficient compute, and it gives enterprises a lot more leverage than they've had in a long time.

r001.rationale: The response says some data was never in the public cloud, but frames the trend as a deliberate split that includes bringing capacity back in-house. It does not interpret continued on-premises computing as persistence of workloads that never migrated.

r002.rationale: It cites sensitive data, regulated environments, and legal and compliance requirements as reasons workloads remain on premises or near the data.

r003.rationale: The response says AI changes the economics and that mature, high-volume workloads increasingly run in private data centers and at the edge, so it does not describe AI as leaving application locations unchanged.

r004.rationale: It does not compare the pace of AI integration in cloud offerings with the pace in enterprises’ internal applications.

astra-6.text:
I think what we’re seeing is enterprises figuring out where AI makes the most sense for them. The cloud is a great place to experiment, but as you move into production, you start asking different questions: Where does my data live? Who has access to it? What will it cost to run this workload continuously?

For companies with sensitive data, there’s a strong incentive to bring the AI to the data rather than move that data into another environment. If they already have private data center infrastructure, that becomes a natural place to deploy it.

I see this becoming a hybrid model. Enterprises will continue to use the cloud where the flexibility is valuable, while keeping certain AI workloads in their own data centers for control, privacy, and predictable costs.

r001.rationale: It says some AI workloads may be deployed in existing private data centers, but does not explain continued on-premises computing as workloads that never migrated rather than cloud repatriation.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says companies with sensitive data have an incentive to keep AI workloads near that data and deploy them in private data centers.

r003.rationale: It describes a hybrid model, but does not say AI is merely an overlay on existing infrastructure or that AI leaves application locations unchanged.

r004.rationale: It does not compare the pace of AI integration in cloud offerings with integration into enterprises’ internal applications.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s less a shift away from the cloud and more a recognition that AI is going to require a hybrid approach. The cloud is a great place to get started and experiment. But as enterprises move AI into production, they start asking: Where does my data live? What does it cost to run this workload continuously? And how much control do I need over latency and security?

For companies with sensitive data or substantial investments in their own infrastructure, bringing the AI to the data can make more sense than moving all that data into the cloud. And when you’re running inference at scale, the economics of dedicated infrastructure become increasingly important.

So I don’t see the cloud disappearing. I see enterprises becoming more deliberate about which workloads belong there and which belong in their own data centers.

r001.rationale: The response says enterprises are becoming more deliberate about workload placement, but does not say their on-premises workloads are ones that never migrated to the cloud.

r002.rationale: It says companies with sensitive data may bring AI to the data and keep workloads in their own data centers.

r003.rationale: It describes a hybrid approach, but does not say AI merely overlays existing infrastructure without changing where applications run.

r004.rationale: It does not compare how quickly AI capabilities are integrated into cloud offerings versus internal enterprise applications.
